title: Should you restart your phone every week?
caption:
The NSA says restart your phone every week. Should you?
A restart can wipe out some spyware. But the NSA's own chart says: sometimes.
Did you restart this week? Yes or no?

how often should you restart your phone

pinned_comment: Short version: a restart can wipe out some spyware, but the NSA's own chart says a weekly restart only "Sometimes prevents" spearphishing and zero-click exploits. In one 2023 iPhone case, Kaspersky said phones "may be reinfected after rebooting." A restart doesn't close the hole; an update can. So update, and restart weekly. Did you restart this week? Yes or no?

pinned_backups.if: So a weekly restart keeps me safe?
pinned_backups.reply: No, it can help, that's all. The NSA's own chart marks "Turn Device Off & On Weekly" as "Sometimes prevents" for spearphishing and zero-click exploits, and "Does not prevent" for every other threat on it. What closes the hole is an update: "Update the device software and applications as soon as possible."

pinned_backups.if: Can my iPhone restart on a schedule?
pinned_backups.reply: We only read Samsung's US page on scheduled restarts, so the video makes no claim about iPhone or Pixel either way. A restart by hand does the same job: the NSA's wording is "Power the device off and on weekly."

Apple's iOS 16.5.1, released June 21, 2023, fixed a kernel flaw (CVE-2023-32434) credited to researchers at Kaspersky. Apple: "this issue may have been actively exploited against versions of iOS released before iOS 15.7." That's one flaw in one case; the habit is to install updates as they come.

pinned_backups.if: My Samsung restarts by itself. Is that this?
pinned_backups.reply: It might be. Samsung's US page: "Auto restart only runs when the device is not being used. By default, the screen must be off and the battery level must be at least 30%." It also says "One UI 8.0 introduced Inactivity restart, which automatically reboots a locked, unused device after 72 hours". Both live under Settings › Device care › Auto optimization › Auto restart.
No. The copy we read is dated Oct 2020, rev 1.1 (U/OO/155488-20 | PP-20-0622). The weekly restart and "Sometimes prevents" are both on it.

Kaspersky called the 2023 campaign "Operation Triangulation": iPhones hit by "a successful zero-click compromise via an iMessage attachment". Kaspersky: "The malicious toolset does not support persistence". It's one case, not proof that a restart clears all spyware.

youtube_description:
The NSA says restart your phone weekly. Its Mobile Device Best Practices sheet says: "Power the device off and on weekly." So should you restart your phone every week?
A restart can wipe out some spyware, but the NSA's own chart says a weekly restart "Sometimes prevents" spearphishing and zero-click exploits. A restart doesn't close the hole; an update can. So update, and restart weekly. On a Samsung Galaxy phone you can set it on a schedule: Settings › Device care › Auto optimization › Auto restart › Restart on schedule.

The NSA sheet ("Mobile Device Best Practices", U/OO/155488-20 | PP-20-0622 | Oct 2020 rev 1.1), page 1: "Power the device off and on weekly." and "Update the device software and applications as soon as possible." Page 2, the chart "WHAT CAN I DO TO PREVENT/MITIGATE?": the column "Turn Device Off & On Weekly" is marked "Sometimes prevents" for "Spearphishing (To install Malware)" and "Zero-Click Exploits"; every other row in that column is "Does not prevent". The chart's three marks are "Does not prevent (no icon)", "Sometimes prevents" and "Almost always prevents".

Why a restart can help: in one 2023 iPhone spyware case, Kaspersky's "Operation Triangulation" report found "a successful zero-click compromise via an iMessage attachment" and said: "The malicious toolset does not support persistence, most likely due to the limitations of the OS. The timelines of multiple devices indicate that they may be reinfected after rebooting." So a reboot can wipe it out, and those iPhones may get infected again.

Why the update matters: Apple's iOS 16.5.1 (released June 21, 2023) fixed a kernel flaw, CVE-2023-32434, credited to researchers at Kaspersky. Apple: "Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been actively exploited against versions of iOS released before iOS 15.7." That is one flaw in one case, not every attack.

Check yours. Samsung US Support: "Tap Auto optimization. Tap Auto restart." "Enable Restart on schedule. Your device will restart automatically on your selected date and time." "Auto restart only runs when the device is not being used. By default, the screen must be off and the battery level must be at least 30%."

Fine print: A restart can help; it doesn't stop every attack, and the NSA lists it as one practice among many. The Kaspersky quotes describe one 2023 iPhone case, not all spyware or Android. Samsung: "Menu names, settings, and screen layouts may vary depending on the model and software version." The film makes no claim about scheduled restarts on iPhone or Pixel. The screens (the search bar, the NSA sheet and chart, the Apple card and the Samsung settings) are re-created by hand, each from its own maker's or agency's wording; the phones are generic, and the bug is a paper symbol, not a real piece of spyware. Not affiliated with NSA, Apple, Samsung or Kaspersky.

Sources:
- NSA, "Mobile Device Best Practices" (U/OO/155488-20, PP-20-0622, Oct 2020 rev 1.1), read Nov 22, 2026: https://media.defense.gov/2021/Sep/16/2002855921/-1/-1/0/MOBILE_DEVICE_BEST_PRACTICES_FINAL_V3%20-%20COPY.PDF
- Kaspersky Securelist, "Operation Triangulation: iOS devices targeted with previously unknown malware" (June 1, 2023), read Nov 22, 2026: https://securelist.com/operation-triangulation/109842/
- Apple Support, "About the security content of iOS 16.5.1 and iPadOS 16.5.1" (103837), read Nov 22, 2026: https://support.apple.com/en-us/103837
- Samsung US Support, "Samsung Galaxy device appears to keep restarting" (TSG10013116), read Nov 22, 2026: https://www.samsung.com/us/support/troubleshoot/TSG10013116/
